turns.human_input: I'm 59 and I've been a senior software engineer at the same company for fourteen years. I'm starting to burn out pretty badly but I genuinely don't want to stop working entirely — I like the mental engagement and I'd lose my mind at home. I've been thinking about what people call phased retirement: maybe dropping to part-time, doing some consulting, or shifting to a less demanding role. I have $820k in a 401k, no pension, my mortgage has 8 years left, and my kids are out of the house. My wife works part-time bringing in about $28k a year. Is a phased approach actually viable for me or is it wishful thinking?
turns.ai_response: Phased retirement is increasingly viable in tech specifically, and your situation — solid asset base, working spouse income, no major dependents — gives you more flexibility than most people at this stage. The path isn't wishful thinking, but the options have meaningfully different financial and practical implications. The most important variable upfront: does your current employer have any history of accommodating reduced-hours arrangements for senior engineers, or is that a non-starter there?

turns.human_input: The part that seems most complicated to me is the healthcare. Right now I have good employer coverage for both of us. If I go part-time or leave for consulting, that goes away. I don't turn 65 for six years. How do other people in this situation handle the health insurance gap, and how expensive is it really?
turns.ai_response:
Healthcare is the right thing to stress-test first, and the answer depends significantly on which path you take.

If your employer offers part-time arrangements with benefits retained — which some large tech companies do for senior engineers transitioning down — you may be able to preserve coverage. That is the cleanest outcome and worth exploring directly with HR before assuming it isn't available.

If you leave for independent consulting or a benefits-ineligible part-time role, you have three realistic options. COBRA continuation from your current employer buys you 18 months at full premium cost — typically $1,800-$2,400/month for a couple your age. That is expensive but buys time to find a longer-term solution. ACA marketplace plans are the primary longer-term answer; with your wife's $28k income and modest 401k distributions, your household MAGI may qualify for meaningful subsidies. The income engineering point matters here: if you control how much you draw from the 401k, you can manage your ACA subsidy eligibility deliberately. A third option is your wife's employer plan if she has access to one — a QSEE or employer-sponsored plan through her part-time employer, if available, could be significantly cheaper than individual market options.

Budget realistically: if you're on ACA without subsidies, plan for $1,500-$2,000/month. With careful income management, you might land at $600-$900/month. The six-year gap to Medicare is long enough that this deserves a dedicated line item in any phased retirement budget.

turns.human_input: I hadn't thought about the income engineering for ACA subsidies — that's actually a significant variable. There's also the question of whether I try to negotiate a part-time arrangement with my current employer versus leaving entirely for consulting. I feel like there are too many interdependent decisions here. Can you map out what the overall phased retirement strategy should look like for me and what order to tackle the decisions?
turns.ai_response:
Here is a sequenced framework for your situation.

Step one, negotiate before you exit. Before making any external moves, have a direct conversation with your manager or HR about a reduced-hours arrangement. At fourteen years and senior engineering level, you have leverage you may not be using. Aim for 60-70% time at proportional salary with benefits retained. This is the highest-value outcome if achievable — it preserves healthcare, maintains 401k contribution eligibility, and lets you test reduced workload without burning bridges. Many engineers in this position are surprised by how receptive employers are when the alternative is losing institutional knowledge entirely.

Step two, run your monthly budget numbers at reduced income. At 60-70% of your current salary plus your wife's $28k, what does your monthly cash flow look like against your actual expenses? The mortgage has eight years left — calculate that payment against the reduced income scenario. If the cash flow works without touching the 401k, your assets continue compounding and your ACA situation is simpler. If it doesn't, you need to draw from somewhere, which changes both the tax picture and the subsidy calculation.

Step three, if the internal negotiation fails, the consulting path requires two parallel preparations: lining up one or two anchor clients before you leave (dramatically reduces income risk), and establishing healthcare continuity through COBRA as a bridge while you assess ACA options based on your actual first-year consulting income.

Step four, regardless of path: do not touch the 401k before 59.5 without a penalty, and even after 59.5, be deliberate about distribution timing for ACA management. You crossed 59.5 this year, so the penalty window is gone, but tax and subsidy management still matter.

The decision order: negotiate internally first. That outcome determines everything downstream.

turns.human_input: I should tell you — I already had the internal conversation six months ago and it went nowhere. My manager was supportive but HR said the company doesn't have a formal part-time track for senior ICs. I didn't push it further, but now I'm wondering if I gave up too easily. Do you think it's worth going back and making a harder push, or is that ship sailed?
turns.ai_response:
It is worth going back, and the framing of the second attempt matters more than whether you push harder in the generic sense.

HR's response that there is no formal part-time track is a policy answer, not a business decision. The person who can override it is not HR — it is your manager's manager or a senior leader who cares about retaining you specifically. A second attempt that goes through the right channel, framed as a retention conversation rather than a benefits question, has a different dynamic.

Consider framing it this way: you are not asking for a policy exception, you are proposing a specific arrangement — defined deliverables, defined hours, defined duration — that allows the company to retain your institutional knowledge during a critical transition period. Offer a 12-month trial. Come with a concrete proposal rather than a request.

The ship is not sailed on this. Six months is not long, you are still employed, and you have not given an ultimatum or signaled departure. The timing is actually reasonable — going back now with a more structured proposal is a credible move, not a retreat.

If the second attempt fails cleanly, you have better information and you can move to the consulting path with less second-guessing. But given that you haven't tried the right channel yet, it's worth one more attempt.

turns.human_input: Assuming the second attempt fails and I go the consulting route — what are the two or three financial moves I should make in the first twelve months to protect myself and set the foundation correctly?
turns.ai_response:
The three highest-priority financial moves in your first twelve months as an independent consultant:

First, establish a solo 401k immediately after leaving. As a self-employed consultant, you can contribute both the employee and employer portions — up to $66,000 annually or your net consulting income, whichever is less. This is dramatically higher than a traditional employee's contribution limit and lets you continue aggressive retirement savings while managing taxable income downward. Lower taxable income also improves your ACA subsidy position. Open the solo 401k account before year-end of your first year to preserve the contribution window.

Second, build a cash buffer of 12 months of fixed expenses before you rely on consulting income for essentials. Consulting income is lumpy, especially in the first year when you are building client relationships. Your $820k in the 401k is not an emergency fund — withdrawing from it to cover slow consulting months has tax and sequencing costs. Identify the cash or near-cash assets you will use as the bridge, and size them deliberately before you leave W-2 employment.

Third, price your consulting work correctly from day one. Independent consultants routinely underprice relative to their W-2 salary because they do not account for self-employment tax (15.3% on the first $160k of net income), benefits they now pay directly, and the non-billable time in running a practice. A rough rule of thumb: your daily consulting rate should be at least 1.5-2x your equivalent W-2 daily rate to break even on a fully loaded cost basis. Getting this wrong in year one creates cash flow pressure that forces bad decisions elsewhere.
